paragraphs.heading: Through the wall
paragraphs.text: Quantum tunnelling, also called barrier penetration, is when something like an electron or an atom gets through an energy barrier that classical mechanics says it cannot cross, since it lacks the energy to get over. A helpful picture is a ball rolling toward a hill. In classical physics, a ball without enough energy to reach the top simply rolls back down. In quantum mechanics, a particle has a small chance of crossing to the other side anyway.

paragraphs.heading: Why it happens
paragraphs.text: Tunnelling follows from the wave nature of matter and from quantum indeterminacy. A particle's state is described by its wave function, and equations such as the Schrödinger equation set how that wave function changes. When a barrier is short and narrow, a small part of the wave function can appear beyond it, and that part is the chance of tunnelling through. When the particle's wave hits the barrier, most of it bounces back and some gets through. Afterwards the wave sits on both sides of the barrier, while the total chance of finding the particle somewhere stays at one.

paragraphs.heading: What makes it likely
paragraphs.text: The chance of getting through falls exponentially as the barrier gets higher or wider, and as the particle gets heavier. That is why tunnelling is most obvious for light particles such as electrons crossing barriers only atoms thick. Even so, it has been observed with protons and even whole atoms.

paragraphs.heading: Where it matters
paragraphs.text: Tunnelling plays an essential part in nuclear fusion and in the alpha decay of atomic nuclei. It is put to use in the tunnel diode, flash memory, quantum computing and the scanning tunnelling microscope. It also sets a limit on microelectronics. Electrons tunnel easily through insulating layers and transistors thinner than about 1 nm, which limits how small devices can be made.

paragraphs.heading: A version with light
paragraphs.text: Light shows a similar effect. Light striking a prism at an angle just past the critical angle is reflected. But if a second prism is brought within a few wavelengths of that reflecting face, some of the light tunnels across the gap.

paragraphs.heading: How it was found
paragraphs.text: The Schrödinger equation appeared in 1926, and in a series of 1927 articles Friedrich Hund was the first to apply it to tunnelling through a barrier between two classically allowed regions. Leonid Mandelstam and Mikhail Leontovich found tunnelling on their own and published in 1928. A great success came in 1928, when George Gamow, and separately Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon, used tunnelling to explain alpha decay mathematically. At first nobody said tunnel effect; people spoke of a particle penetrating, or leaking through, a barrier.
